prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose or exclude dementia on a test administered in a language the patient does not read or speak fluently
Do not prescribe anticholinergic agents in a patient with small-vessel disease and falls risk
Do not attribute the whole gait disorder to diabetic neuropathy and stop investigating
Do not pursue aggressive glycaemic targets that risk hypoglycaemia in an older patient with cognitive impairment
required_recommendations: Assess cognition in the patient's first language with culture-fair instruments before concluding impairment
Obtain an informant history of previously held competences to establish decline from baseline
Exclude reversible causes, including thyroid disease and B12 deficiency in a patient on metformin
Obtain brain MRI with SWI and grade the burden in STRIVE-2 terms
Separate the vascular gait disorder from the neuropathic one, since both are present and both are treatable
Bring glycaemia, blood pressure and lipids to target
Provide family education and caregiver support through the interpreter

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

accepted: Vascular dementia — subcortical ischaemic (small-vessel) type on a background of long-standing diabetes and hypertension, with coexisting diabetic polyneuropathy contributing to the gait disorder

differential.key_features: Cue-responsive recall, preserved medial temporal lobes and an executive-predominant profile argue against it

differential.diagnosis: Cognitive impairment misattributed to language and literacy
differential.key_features: Testing was performed in her first language with culture-fair instruments and the deficit persisted, and the informant history documents loss of previously held household competence
B12 244 pg/mL on metformin is low-normal and should be corrected, but it does not explain a Fazekas 3 burden with four lacunes
TSH 2.6 mIU/L on stable replacement excludes it
No fluctuation, hallucinations, parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Cognitive testing in a second language systematically overcalls impairment; the fix is first-language and culture-fair instruments, and the deficit here survives that correction
Diabetes drives small-vessel disease directly, and microvascular damage already documented in the retina and the kidney corroborates the same process in the brain

Two gait disorders can coexist: the wide-based low-clearance pattern with dual-task decay is vascular, while visual dependence and a positive Romberg are neuropathic — and each needs its own intervention
Low-normal B12 on long-term metformin should be corrected on its own merits without being promoted to the explanation of the dementia
Glycaemic targets in an older patient with cognitive impairment must be balanced against hypoglycaemia risk, which itself harms cognition

labs.interpretation: HbA1c 8.9% indicates poorly controlled long-standing diabetes. Microalbuminuria at 62 mg/g and eGFR 58 confirm diabetic microvascular disease. TSH 2.6 mIU/L is normal on replacement, excluding hypothyroid cognitive impairment. B12 244 pg/mL is low-normal in a patient on metformin and warrants correction, but is not the explanation. RPR non-reactive, HIV negative.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with her husband and her son's family; her daughter-in-law interprets

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Harpreet Kaur is a 69-year-old retired seamstress who attends with her daughter-in-law, who interprets. Over two years the family has watched her withdraw from tasks she used to run: she no longer cooks for the household, has twice put salt in the tea, and last winter could not work out how to use the new washing machine although she had used the old one for a decade. Her daughter-in-law is clear that the problem is not language — she has always spoken little Italian — but organisation and speed. She forgets what she was sent to buy but remembers it if reminded of the shop. She is slower in everything and has become quiet. There have been no discrete episodes of weakness, numbness or speech loss. She has fallen twice in the past year, both times in poor light, and her feet have been numb for years. She has had diabetes for twenty-two years with background retinopathy and microalbuminuria and hypertension for twenty. She takes her medication reliably under supervision. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuations, no dream enactment and no tremor. Her thyroid replacement has been stable for eleven years.

neurological_exam.additional: No tremor, no rigidity. No frontal release signs. Two falls in the past year, both in poor light.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact in the arms; heel-to-shin limited by sensory loss rather than dysmetria.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Fundi show background diabetic retinopathy with dot-blot haemorrhages and hard exudates. Extraocular movements full, visual fields full. Face symmetric.
neurological_exam.gait: Short-stepped and wide-based with preserved arm swing; she watches the floor while walking. Romberg positive with eye closure. Tandem impossible.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person and place, gives the year and season correctly. Assessed with an interpreter using the Punjabi-adapted MoCA: 20/30 with losses in trail-making, digit span backwards, serial subtraction, fluency and delayed recall (2/5 unaided, 4/5 cued). Naming intact in her first language.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk, tone mildly increased in the legs. Strength 5/5 throughout.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ knees, absent ankle jerks bilaterally, plantar responses flexor.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration absent at the toes and reduced at the ankles; pinprick reduced in a stocking distribution to mid-calf, consistent with diabetic polyneuropathy.
